intro:
These exercises turn the chapter's binary-contract discipline into reflexes. Each one forces the same decision the chapter opened with: a type either has a stable, agreed-upon shape that may cross a C ABI seam, or it is a Rust-specific representation whose layout must stay behind it. The warm-up sorts types into those two buckets, the code-reading exercises trace the two runnable listings layer by layer, and the implementation and debugging exercises make you write the guard sequences, ownership shapes, and panic policy by hand.

The through-line is that the compiler checks nothing across the seam. Calling convention, layout, who frees what, how long a pointer stays valid, and what happens on failure are all things you assert and must get right yourself. The design exercise closes the loop by routing a real legacy-C++ integration through the chapter's decision tree, where the tool you pick changes only how much boilerplate is generated, never the ownership, panic, and ABI-stability contract you still owe.

exerciseSolutions.title: Sort types into what may cross the seam
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The decisive question for each type is whether both languages already agree on its in-memory representation. If they do, it may cross unchanged. If the shape is a Rust implementation detail, it must be flattened into pointers, lengths, and integers before it reaches the boundary.

Crossable unchanged: i32 (a fixed-width integer the C ABI already names), *const i32 paired with a usize length (a raw address plus a count, exactly the lowered form of a slice), *mut i64 (a raw writable address, the canonical out-parameter shape), and an opaque handle pointer (a *mut to a type the foreign side never inspects the fields of). These are all addresses and integers with a stable layout.

Must stay behind the seam: &str, Vec<u8>, and Result<u32, MyError>. A &str is a two-word slice (pointer plus length) that additionally carries a lifetime and a UTF-8 validity promise; its layout is not guaranteed across compiler versions and the lifetime has no C expression. Flatten it to *const u8 plus a usize length (and document the encoding). A Vec<u8> is a three-word owning structure (pointer, length, capacity) tied to Rust's allocator; even though it describes contiguous bytes, the foreign side cannot honor the capacity field or the allocator contract, so passing it would invite a mismatched free. Lower it to *const u8 (or *mut u8) plus a usize length, and keep ownership and freeing on one side via an explicit destroy function. A Result<u32, MyError> has no fixed discriminant layout and no agreed-upon error representation, so it becomes an integer status as the return value with the u32 payload delivered through a caller-owned out parameter (*mut u32) on the success path.

The reason &str and Vec<u8> cannot cross even though they are contiguous bytes is layout, not content: a slice or owning vector has no fixed, agreed-upon C representation, and the aliasing, lifetime, and allocator promises they encode cannot be expressed or honored on the C side.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The two buckets: rich Rust types stay behind the seam; flattened pointer/length/integer shapes cross it.
criteria: i32, *const i32 with usize length, *mut i64, and the opaque handle pointer are listed as crossable because each is a fixed-width integer or raw address with a stable layout.
&str, Vec<u8>, and Result are identified as Rust-specific representations that may not cross unchanged.
&str/Vec<u8> are replaced by a raw pointer plus an explicit length, and Result by an integer status plus out parameters.
The stated reason is layout: a slice, owning vector, or Result has no fixed, agreed-upon C representation.

exerciseSolutions.title: Trace the three layers of the abs wrapper
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Example 1 is deliberately split into three layers so the unsafe surface is as small as possible. The foreign symbol is ffi_demo_abs, defined in the c_shim module with extern "C" and no_mangle and reached through an unsafe extern "C" declaration block. The middle layer is the one-line wrapper safe_abs, which performs the actual call inside an unsafe block and documents why it is sound. The top layer is main, which only ever calls safe_abs and never sees a raw call. Only safe_abs holds an unsafe block; the foreign declaration and main both stay safe.

The unsafe extern "C" declaration tells the compiler two things: a symbol named ffi_demo_abs exists somewhere else, and it must be called with the C calling convention rather than Rust's unspecified one. What it does not verify is that the foreign side actually honors that signature. The compiler cannot check that the real ffi_demo_abs takes an i32, returns an i32, has the claimed name, or even exists until link time; asserting the contract is the programmer's job, which is why the call is unsafe.

The seam requires no ownership transfer because the signature is plain i32 -> i32. Both the argument and the result are Copy, fixed-width integers passed by value. Nothing is allocated, nothing is borrowed across the boundary, and nothing needs to be freed afterward, so the only soundness obligation is the calling convention itself. That is exactly what the SAFETY comment records.

If the body used abs instead of wrapping_abs, the input i32::MIN would be a boundary hazard. The absolute value of i32::MIN is 2147483648, which does not fit in i32, so abs panics in debug builds (and the operation is otherwise an overflow). A panic unwinding out of an extern "C" function and across the C ABI boundary is undefined behavior, because the foreign caller's frames were not compiled to be unwound through. wrapping_abs avoids this by defining the result on the whole input range: wrapping_abs on i32::MIN returns i32::MIN, so the function always returns a value and never unwinds. Even a trivial exported function needs a panic policy at the boundary, and this is it.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Three layers with unsafe isolated to safe_abs; wrapping_abs supplies the boundary's panic policy.
criteria: The three layers are named (foreign declaration, unsafe wrapper safe_abs, safe main) with only safe_abs holding unsafe.
The declaration is described as asserting the symbol and signature exist elsewhere, which the compiler cannot check on the foreign side.
The seam is shown to be plain i32 -> i32 by value, so nothing is allocated or freed across it.
abs on i32::MIN is shown to panic and an unwind across the C ABI is undefined behavior, which wrapping_abs avoids.

exerciseSolutions.title: Export a length-prefixed buffer reader
exerciseSolutions.solution:
This follows the guard-sequence shape of sum_i32s from Example 2: validate the out pointer first, then the input pointer, each returning a distinct nonzero status before any dereference, and only build the slice once both pointers are known non-null. The signature is exactly fn max_i32(ptr: *const i32, len: usize, out_max: *mut i32) -> i32, marked extern "C" with no_mangle so the symbol is exported under a stable, unmangled name.

Order matters. Check out_max first and return status 1 if it is null, because writing the result through a null out parameter would be undefined behavior regardless of the input. Then check ptr and return status 2 if it is null. These checks happen before any raw read or write, so a null from either side is reported as a value the caller can branch on rather than a crash.

The empty-input case is a contract decision, not a free pass. std::slice::from_raw_parts requires a non-null, aligned pointer even when len is 0, and there is no defined maximum of zero elements. Rather than read from an empty slice or write a garbage maximum, the function returns a distinct nonzero status (3) for len == 0 and documents it. The caller now knows that status 3 means "no elements, no maximum produced" and that *out_max was left untouched.

Only after the out pointer is non-null, the input pointer is non-null, and len is at least 1 does the function build the slice inside an unsafe block with a SAFETY comment, compute the maximum (max() on a non-empty slice yields Some, which is safe to unwrap here because emptiness was already ruled out, though using a fold avoids the unwrap entirely), and write it through *out_max on the success path before returning 0. On every failure path *out_max is never written, so the caller's storage is never corrupted by a failed call.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Guard out pointer, then input pointer, then empty input; the slice and the write happen only on the validated success path.
criteria: The signature is exactly fn max_i32(ptr: *const i32, len: usize, out_max: *mut i32) -> i32 and is marked extern "C".
Null out_max returns status 1 and null ptr returns status 2, each a distinct nonzero status checked before any dereference.
len == 0 returns a defined nonzero status (3) and leaves *out_max untouched rather than reading an empty slice or writing garbage.
The slice is built inside an unsafe block with a SAFETY comment, and *out_max is written only on the success path before returning 0.

exerciseSolutions.title: Map ownership across the seam with an opaque handle
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Ownership has no syntax in C, so the surface expresses it by choosing fixed pointer shapes. Here Rust owns the allocation; the caller only ever holds an opaque *mut CounterHandle and must call destroy exactly once. The Rust struct behind the handle never appears in any C signature: the four exported functions speak only in the opaque pointer, integers, and out parameters.

create boxes the Rust struct and hands ownership out as a raw pointer with Box::into_raw. This allocates on Rust's heap and deliberately leaks the Box so the allocation outlives the call; the returned pointer is the handle. increment and read each take the raw handle, null-check it, and reconstruct a borrow with unsafe { &mut *handle } or unsafe { &*handle } without taking ownership. They must not reconstruct a Box, because that would free the allocation on return. read uses an out parameter for the value and returns an integer status so its contract matches the rest of the seam.

destroy is the matching reclaim: it null-checks the handle and then calls Box::from_raw exactly once, turning the raw pointer back into an owned Box that is dropped at the end of the function. Box::into_raw and Box::from_raw must be paired one-to-one; calling from_raw twice on the same pointer is a double free, and never calling it leaks the allocation. After destroy returns, the caller's handle is dangling and must not be used again, which is part of the documented contract.

The comment on the surface records the ownership rules so they are readable from the signatures: Rust allocates and owns the counter, the caller holds the handle and may mutate through increment or read through read, and only destroy frees it, exactly once. An opaque handle is just a pointer to a type whose fields the foreign side never sees, which is what keeps the richer Rust model behind the seam.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: create/into_raw, borrow-only increment/read, and destroy/from_raw form a one-to-one allocate-and-free pair across the opaque handle.
criteria: The four extern "C" functions expose only the opaque *mut CounterHandle, integers, and out parameters, never the Rust struct by value.
create uses Box::into_raw and destroy uses Box::from_raw exactly once, dropping the reclaimed Box.
increment and read null-check the handle and reconstruct a borrow (&mut */&*) without freeing it.
A comment records that Rust owns the allocation, the caller holds the handle, and only destroy frees it.

exerciseSolutions.title: Stop an unwind from crossing the boundary
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is not a wrong value but a path on which the function can unwind out of an extern "C" frame. A Rust panic crossing the C ABI boundary is undefined behavior because the foreign caller's frames were not compiled to be unwound through, and it tends to crash far from the cause. The fix is to remove every panicking operation and report failure as a distinct integer status before control leaves the function.

The panic sources in a body that parses a caller buffer are: indexing such as buf[0] or buf[i] (panics on out-of-bounds), slicing such as &buf[..n] (panics if n exceeds the length), unwrap on the parse Result (panics on malformed input), and raw arithmetic that can overflow (panics in debug builds). Each is a boundary hazard because the panic does not stay inside Rust; it unwinds toward the foreign caller.

The refactor replaces each panicking operation with a checked form that yields a status instead. Indexing becomes buf.get(i), which returns Option and lets a None map to a nonzero status. Slicing becomes get(range) or an explicit length check before slicing. The parse stays as a Result and is matched, never unwrapped, mapping Err to a distinct status. Raw arithmetic becomes checked_add (and friends), mapping the overflow None to a status. Every failure becomes a distinct nonzero return code the caller can branch on, and the successful value is delivered through an out parameter.

Whether to also wrap the body in std::panic::catch_unwind is a judgment call. Once the panicking operations are gone, catch_unwind is a backstop, not the primary fix: it converts any panic that still slips through (for example from a helper you do not control, or a debug-only overflow you missed) into a caught error instead of undefined behavior. It is cheap insurance at the outer edge of the exported function, but it must not be a substitute for removing the panics, because relying on it alone leaves the real hazards in place and obscures the contract. The rule stated plainly: no cross-language unwinding; translate failure to an integer status before control crosses the boundary. With the checked forms in place, every path returns a status and the function cannot unwind.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Each indexing/slicing/unwrap/arithmetic panic is replaced by a checked form mapped to a status; catch_unwind is only the outer backstop.
criteria: Indexing, slicing, unwrap, and overflowing arithmetic are each named and replaced with get, a bound check, a matched Result, and checked_add.
Every failure is reported through a distinct nonzero status code, never by panicking.
The answer states the rule plainly: no cross-language unwinding; translate failure to a status before control leaves the function.
catch_unwind is used as an explicit backstop, with the primary fix being removal of the panics.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose a binding tool for a legacy C++ subsystem
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The chapter's decision tree turns on two questions: do you control both sides of the boundary, and how large is the C++ surface you need to reach. For this scenario the answers are: you do not fully control both sides (you own the Rust side but not the historical C++ headers), and the C++ surface is large (a legacy subsystem reached through an existing host process, plugin loader, and native test harness).

Given a large C++ surface you do not control, the recommendation is a deliberate C ABI seam: a hand-written C shim that exposes a narrow, stable extern "C" contract, with bindgen used to generate the Rust declarations for that shim's C header rather than for the raw C++ headers. cxx and autocxx are strongest when you control both sides and want a curated, ongoing C++/Rust bridge that tracks the C++ types directly; here you do not own the historical headers and the requirement is explicitly a narrow ABI contract, not a broad type-level bridge. autocxx attempting to consume a large legacy C++ surface you cannot modify tends to drag in template, exception, and standard-library assumptions you were specifically asked to keep out. The hand-written C shim plus bindgen keeps the contract surface small: layout, pointer validity, ownership, status-code errors, and no cross-language unwinding are all stated explicitly at one thin seam. "C++ integration" here is, correctly, a deliberate C ABI seam around C++ code, which buys a smaller contract and fewer compiler- and standard-library assumptions.

What the tool does not write for you is the contract itself. bindgen generates Rust signatures from the C header, but it does not decide who allocates and who frees, does not establish how long each pointer stays valid, does not convert C++ exceptions or Rust panics into status codes, and does not guarantee the ABI stays stable across compiler versions. Those obligations remain yours: the tool reduces boilerplate, not responsibility. You still author the shim's ownership rules (opaque handles with explicit create/destroy), the status-code error mapping, and the no-unwind policy on both directions of the seam.

To test and sanitize the layer before shipping, exercise the seam under the existing native test harness so it is driven exactly as production drives it, and build that harness with sanitizers: AddressSanitizer to catch use-after-free, double free, and out-of-bounds across the boundary; and where available a leak detector to confirm every create is matched by a destroy and that into_raw/from_raw stay paired. Add targeted tests for each status code and each null path, a round-trip ownership test that creates, mutates, reads, and destroys a handle, and a deliberate fault-injection test that confirms a forced error returns a status rather than unwinding. Miri can validate the Rust-side unsafe blocks in isolation. The combination proves both the values and the contract: that nothing leaks, nothing is freed twice, and no unwind crosses the seam.
criteria: The choice is framed around the two decision-tree questions: whether you control both sides (no) and how large the C++ surface is (large).
A hand-written C shim plus bindgen is recommended specifically because the C++ surface is large and you do not fully control it, with cxx/autocxx ruled out.
The answer states the tool reduces boilerplate but does not change the ownership, panic, and ABI-stability contract you still owe.
A concrete plan exercises the seam under the native harness with sanitizer (ASan/leak) builds, plus per-status, null-path, round-trip, and fault-injection tests.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
status = 0
total = 12
null input status = 2
null out status = 1
labSolution.explanation:
The lab models the exported sum_i32s seam from Example 2 in plain std Rust. The two raw-pointer parameters are stood in by Option<&[i32]> and Option<&mut i64>: a None models a null pointer, and a Some models a validated, borrowed pointer. The caller owns both the input array and the output slot; the function only borrows them for the duration of the call, exactly as the C ABI version borrows the caller's buffer and out storage.

The body is a guard sequence in the chapter's fixed order. It checks the out parameter first, returning STATUS_NULL_OUT (1) if it is None, because there is no defined place to write a result without it. It then checks the input, returning STATUS_NULL_INPUT (2) if it is None. Only once both are present does it do the real work: each i32 is widened to i64 before summing, so the boundary contract cannot overflow i32, and the total is written through the out parameter before STATUS_OK (0) is returned. Failure is reported as a distinct integer status rather than a Result, which is what keeps the seam portable to C.

The expected output follows directly. The first call passes both pointers and the slice [3, 4, 5], so it returns status 0 and writes 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 into total, printing status = 0 and total = 12. The null-input call returns 2 and the null-out call returns 1, matching the two guard branches.

reviewAnswers.question: What are the four FFI fundamentals the chapter says almost every Rust interop layer is built from?
reviewAnswers.answer: They are the small set of primitives that turn an internal Rust function into a symbol another language can call without guessing about representation: the C calling convention via extern "C", unmangled exported symbol names via no_mangle, C-friendly layout for any shared data (raw buffers and lengths, or opaque handles, instead of Rust ownership types), and integer status codes with out parameters in place of Result. Together they form the thin, stable contract at the seam. Everything richer stays behind it.

reviewAnswers.question: Why must a Rust Result<T, E> be re-expressed as an integer status plus out parameters before crossing a C ABI boundary?
reviewAnswers.answer: A Result<T, E> is a Rust enum with no fixed, agreed-upon C layout: its discriminant representation is an implementation detail and its E type has no C expression, so the foreign side cannot read it. The conventional lowering is therefore an integer status as the return value, with any successful payload delivered through a caller-owned out parameter on the success path. This keeps the contract portable and lets the caller branch on a status code without ever seeing Rust's Result shape.

reviewAnswers.question: What does no_mangle and the extern "C" calling convention each contribute when exporting a Rust function to C or C++?
reviewAnswers.answer: extern "C" sets the calling convention, so the function is called the way C expects (argument passing, register and stack discipline) rather than with Rust's unspecified convention. no_mangle keeps the symbol's name exactly as written instead of applying Rust's name mangling, so the linker on the C or C++ side can find it by that name. You need both: the right convention so the call works, and a stable, predictable name so the symbol can be resolved.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is an in-flight unwind, a Rust panic or a C++ exception, more dangerous to let cross the seam than a bad value?
reviewAnswers.answer: An unwind crossing into frames the other language did not compile to be unwound through is undefined behavior, not merely a wrong result. The foreign frames have no registered cleanup for that unwinding mechanism, so destructors may not run, invariants are left broken, and the program tends to crash far from the cause, making it hard to diagnose. A bad value can at least be checked and rejected; an in-flight unwind corrupts control flow itself. The conservative, operable rule is no cross-language unwinding: translate failure to an integer status or explicit error object before control crosses the boundary.

reviewAnswers.question: Which two questions drive the choice between a hand-written C shim, bindgen, cxx, and autocxx?
reviewAnswers.answer: Whether you control both sides of the boundary, and how large the C++ surface you need to reach is. When you control both sides and want a curated, type-level C++/Rust bridge, cxx (or autocxx for a larger generated surface) fits; when you do not control the C++ headers and need a narrow, stable contract, a deliberate C ABI seam (a hand-written C shim, with bindgen generating the Rust declarations from its header) keeps the surface small. None of these tools changes the contract you owe; they only change how much of the boilerplate is generated for you.
